extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulewriters, state environmental agencies, regulated sources, and stakeholders participating in CAA section 111(d) rulemakings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how the EPA determines the "best system of emission reduction" (BSER), the achievable degree of emission limitation, and the requirements for EPA emission guidelines and state plans under CAA section 111 (including considerations of cost, achievability, non-air impacts, lead time, and RULOF).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately demonstrated (availability) of technology
rubrics_metrics.description: To be considered 'available' the technology may not be one which constitutes a purely theoretical or experimental means of preventing or controlling air pollution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history implies EPA's determination may be technology-forcing; Congress did not intend the technology already be in widespread commercial use. EPA may identify technologies that are not yet widely adopted, so long as they are not purely theoretical or experimental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reasonable projection/extrapolation from data
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequately demonstrated standard of performance may reflect the EPA's reasonable projection of what that particular system may be expected to achieve going forward, extrapolating from available data from pilot projects or individual commercial-scale sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (e.g., Essex Chem. Corp. v. Ruckelshaus) upholds standards based on extrapolation even where the system had not regularly achieved the standard; EPA may extrapolate from testing at one kind of source to related sources (Lignite Energy Council), but may not base determinations on mere speculation when data are unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: No mere speculation—use qualitative methods to address data shortages
rubrics_metrics.description: Where data are unavailable, EPA may not base its determination that a technology is adequately demonstrated or that a standard is achievable on mere speculation or conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA may compensate for limited data through other qualitative methods, including reasonable extrapolation of performance in other industries; must avoid conjectural bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance timeframe and lead time feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must demonstrate that the industry can deploy the technology at scale in the compliance timeframe; section 111 allows for lead time recognizing the need to design, acquire, install, test, and begin operating complex control systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA typically allows phased compliance (e.g., 5-year stepped compliance for residential wood heaters; 1-year lead times for certain equipment; 24 months between FR publication and requirement start). 40 CFR 60.8/60.11 establish timing for performance tests (within 60–180 days after startup). EPA should account for equipment availability, skilled labor, materials, and other practical constraints when setting compliance schedules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost of achieving the emission reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Under CAA section 111(a)(1), EPA is required to take into account 'the cost of achieving [the emission] reduction' when determining the BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have characterized the standard as prohibiting 'excessive' or 'unreasonable' costs, but EPA has discretion in weighing costs with other factors. EPA commonly uses cost-effectiveness metrics ($/ton removed) and, for power sector rules, $/MWh increases to compare costs across industries and evaluate reasonableness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-air quality health and environmental impacts and energy requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must take into account 'any nonair quality health and environmental impact and energy requirements' in determining the BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider impacts such as disposal of control byproducts, water requirements of controls, and impacts of controls on sources' energy needs; courts have required consideration of 'counter-productive environmental effects' (Portland Cement Ass'n v. Ruckelshaus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sector-, regional-, or national-level consideration of factors
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may consider the factors it is required to consider on a national or regional level and over time—not only on a plant-specific level at the time of rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history and case law permit EPA to take a long-term, broad view of costs, environmental and energy effects, and to balance national/regional impacts (e.g., system reliability) when identifying BSER; EPA may reject controls that would create reliability risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-factor balancing of what is 'best'
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'best' authorizes EPA to balance multiple concerns—environmental benefit, energy needs, and economic disruption—when choosing the BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts grant EPA broad discretion to weigh emission reductions, cost of controls, non-air impacts, energy requirements, and other factors that further CAA purposes. EPA must engage in reasoned decisionmaking and may give different weight to factors across different rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of amount of emissions reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must consider the quantity of emissions at issue and the amount of emission reductions a system would yield when determining the 'best system of emission reduction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amount of emission reductions is a logical and required factor to weigh in selecting BSER; EPA may treat this both as statutory mandate and as discretionary consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of technological innovation and expansion
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is required to consider technological innovation as one of the factors in determining the BSER; CAA section 111 is intended to create incentives for new technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress designed section 111 to (1) allow development of technologies that may be treated as adequately demonstrated, (2) expand use of best demonstrated technology, and (3) promote development of emerging technology. EPA may reasonably consider innovation as part of what is 'best.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Achievability of degree of emission limitation (new sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: For new sources, a standard of performance is 'achievable' if a technology can reasonably be projected to be available to an individual source at the time it is constructed that will allow it to meet the standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An achievable standard need not have been routinely achieved prior to adoption, but it must be within the realm of the adequately demonstrated system's efficiency and capable of being met under most reasonably expected adverse conditions. To show achievability EPA must (1) identify variable conditions that might affect expected emissions, and (2) establish that test data relied on are representative of potential industry-wide performance given the range of variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical feasibility for existing sources and RULOF allowance
rubrics_metrics.description: For existing sources under CAA section 111(d), EPA must determine the degree of emission limitation achievable through application of the BSER and provide emission guidelines; states applying standards to particular sources may take into account remaining useful life and other factors (RULOF) when applying less stringent standards or longer compliance schedules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To apply less stringent standards or extended schedules, the state must demonstrate for each facility (or class) that it cannot reasonably achieve the EPA-determined degree of limitation due to unreasonable cost from plant age/location/process design, physical impossibility or technical infeasibility of installing controls, or other facility-specific circumstances. The state must show fundamental differences between facility-specific information and that considered by EPA.

rubrics_metrics.name: States may adopt more stringent standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Under CAA section 116, states may establish standards of performance that are more stringent than EPA's presumptive standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States include their chosen standards in plans submitted to EPA for review; EPA approves satisfactory plans, or may promulgate a Federal plan if a state fails to submit a satisfactory plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emission guideline format: specify BSER and degree of limitation (not only ranges)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's emission guidelines must reflect the degree of emission limitation achievable through application of the BSER, taking into account cost and non-air impacts; the Agency should specifically identify the BSER and the 'degree of emission limitation achievable,' rather than only providing a broad range of values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACE Rule was criticized/repealed in part because it described only a broad range of values as the degree achievable and did not provide adequate guidance for states on the specific degree of limitation needed for an approvable state plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: State plan and unit-specific data and evaluations
rubrics_metrics.description: When states adopt standards of performance under EPA emission guidelines, they must evaluate designated facilities on a source-by-source or group basis and provide summaries including degree of emission limitation achievable through candidate technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACE Rule required states to provide information for each plant: annual generation, CO2 emissions, fuel use/price/carbon content, operation and maintenance costs, heat rates, electric generating capacity, timeline for implementation, and unit-specific evaluations of HRI potential, technical feasibility, and applicability. EPA uses such data to review whether a plan is 'satisfactory.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cost-effectiveness and output-based metrics for reasonableness
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may use cost-effectiveness ($/ton removed) and output-relative metrics ($/MWh) to assess the cost reasonableness of final requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These metrics allow comparison of costs across rules, pollutants, and industries; EPA has used both in prior rulemakings (e.g., NSPS for GHG and VOC from oil and natural gas; Good Neighbor Plan $/MWh).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of updated factual developments and unintended effects
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must consider new factual developments (industry changes, cost developments, subsidies, updated technical reports) and potential unintended consequences (e.g., 'rebound effect') when evaluating whether a prior BSER remains appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACE Rule repeal was based in part on new evidence (updated Sargent & Lundy report, federal subsidies, industry changes) showing prior HRI estimates overstated reductions and that rebound effects could increase CO2. Rulemaking should account for such updated evidence and modeling of unintended consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible bases for repealing a prior rule
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may repeal a prior rule if (1) the selected BSER is not appropriate, (2) new factual developments undermine the prior rationale, or (3) the prior rule failed to specifically identify the BSER or degree of emission limitation thereby not providing adequate guidance to states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each of these grounds alone may justify repeal. Repeal rationale should be supported by technical and legal explanation demonstrating why the prior rule no longer stands or was legally deficient.
